handbook-ironworking-text:
Ironworking Expanded is the iron tier: everything you need to smelt iron in bulk before you own a single boiler. It is deliberately self-sufficient - the whole chain runs off an axle and a waterwheel, and nothing in it needs steam.

The loop. Crushed iron ore and lime flux go into a Burdenmaker, which drops them together into burden - the ore-bearing charge. Burden and coke are then charged into the Cold Blast Furnace through a Tall Hopper, as alternating layers rather than as a mixture. The furnace is blown with cold air from a Twin-Tub Blower and renders the charge down to molten pig iron and slag. The pig runs out of a tap into a molten canal, which plumbs it to wherever you want to cast it.

Pig iron is not a finished metal. It is hard, brittle and useless for tools - it is the shared intermediate everything downstream is made from. Remelt it in a Cupola Furnace - pig and scrap iron go straight in, layered with coke, no preparation needed - and you get cast iron, which casts into machine parts and substitutes for vanilla iron in build recipes. Work it down instead and you get wrought iron, which is vanilla iron. Steel comes later, and needs the steam tier.

What the iron tier leaves behind. Plated pipe - the first of three pipe tiers - and the molten-canal network, both of which every later tier builds on. Cast iron tools and parts. And slag, which is not waste: it lays as paths, slabs and stairs.

Where to start. Build the burdenmaker first - nothing else works without burden, and it asks for nothing but fired brick and no power at all. Then the furnace, then a blower on an axle. The canal can wait: pig solidifies at the tap and can be chiselled out by hand until you have somewhere better to send it.
handbook-orehandling-text:
The furnace does not eat ore. It eats burden - crushed iron ore blended with lime flux - and it eats coke, and the two go in as separate layers. Nothing is premixed. The coke layers are what the blast breathes through; a shaft packed with one homogeneous material chokes.

The Burdenmaker is where burden is made. It is a brick stock house - two hoppers over one shared basin, with a sliding gate between them - and it needs no power at all, so you can build it before you own an axle. The wide hopper takes crushed iron ore; the narrow one takes lime. rightmouse adds one, ctrl + rightmouse adds a stack, and an empty hand takes it back out. Nothing is locked and nothing is spent until you say so.

Open the gate - the centre cell at the base, on the open side - and the single lid draws back, dropping both hoppers into the basin at once as one batch of burden. Reach into the basin to take it out. The basin must be empty before the next batch; that refusal is the only batch boundary this machine has, and it is what keeps two loads from averaging into each other.

Flux is burden's only quality. Block-info shows what is in each hopper and what the pair would make, named under-fluxed, standard or over-fluxed - about one part lime in twenty is standard. The grade is stamped onto the burden that comes out and travels with it, so the furnace can tell you what it is being fed.

Blocks required:
- 1 x Burdenmaker (any burned-brick colour)
- 1 x Tall Hopper, over the furnace shaft

Charging is done in rounds. The tall hopper holds one material at a time, and that is deliberate: one load lays one band. Fill it with coke and let it drip, then fill it with burden. Coke under burden, round after round, until the shaft is full. Block-info on the furnace names the course you are working on and tells you whether the charge as laid will melt or chill.

A furnace lights on a complete round, not on a quantity. The blast has to have something in front of every tuyere, so what the fire waits for is a full bottom course - charge across the whole shaft, not a heap piled down one side.

How you charge decides how hard the furnace is to blow. The blast has to get through the whole column. A coke-lean charge packs dense and demands far more pressure than a hand-driven blower can raise; a coke-rich one blows easily and eats fuel. At the iron tier you charge generously and accept the fuel cost - running lean is what the steam tier is for.

Charging a furnace that is already burning. A new layer with coke in it catches and joins the fire. Burden on its own does not - it sits there cold on top of a hot furnace, plainly unlit. Lay whole rounds and the question never comes up.

Coke, not coal. Coke is baked from coal in a coke oven; raw coal is not fuel here at all. Charcoal is accepted and carries half the carbon of coke, so a shaft charged with it runs cooler for the same layers. Crush iron ore in a pulverizer - even scrap iron bits crush back into crushed iron and go round again.

Nothing is destroyed. Break the burdenmaker and both hoppers, the basin and the brick all come back.
handbook-coldblastfurnace-text:
The Cold Blast Furnace is the iron tier's primary smelter: a tall open-topped stack of refractory brick that reduces ore burden to molten pig iron. It smelts ore and only ore - it will not take scrap. For that you want the cupola.

Building it. Place the Cold Blast Furnace Core first - it is the bottom-centre anchor the whole build hangs off - then ctrl + shift + rightmouse it to see the build outline, and fill in every highlighted block until it reports complete.

Blocks required:
- Refractory Bricks (any tier; the core takes on the tier you build it from)
- 1 x Cold Blast Furnace Core (the anchor, placed first)
- 2 x Tuyere, low on the shaft
- 1 x Iron Tap, low in the hearth wall, and 1 x Slag Tap, higher in the same wall
- 1 x Tall Hopper, over the shaft
The shaft inside is left hollow. That is where the burden goes.

There is no door. The open top of the stack is its chimney - the furnace vents straight up and recycles nothing, which is exactly what makes it the cold blast furnace. A finished furnace is cleared by breaking its walls. Do not stand on the charge: a player who falls into a working furnace does not come out.

Blowing it. The two tuyeres are pipe nodes - run plated pipe from a Twin-Tub Blower to them and the blower will fill the line. How much pressure the furnace needs depends on the charge: a coke-rich burden blows through easily, a lean one packs dense and needs more than a mechanical blower can raise. If the line will not hold pressure, check that the run is sealed - an open pipe end vents to atmosphere.

Firing it. Let the hopper fill the shaft, ignite the burden, and the furnace climbs on its own. It has no fixed maximum temperature: what it reaches is a balance between the heat the coke and the blast put in, and what the stack radiates away and the cold charge soaks up. A rich burden on cold blast settles comfortably past iron's 1482 C melting line. A lean one stalls short of it, and no amount of patience will help - it needs preheated blast, which needs the steam tier.

Block-info always shows the current temperature, the threshold it is trying to clear, and both sides of the ledger, so a stall reads as a number and not as a mystery.

Tapping it. Once it is Melting, molten pig collects behind the iron tap and slag behind the slag tap above it. Open a tap and the metal runs out. With nothing plumbed to it, it solidifies at the tap and is chiselled free by hand; with a molten canal under it, it runs off to be cast properly.

The fire is fragile. Running out of burden, choking the tuyeres, or letting the blast die all count against the furnace, and enough of it puts the fire out.
handbook-moltencanals-text:
Molten metal is plumbed, not carried. You never pick liquid iron up. It leaves a furnace tap into a molten canal and flows, cell by cell, to wherever you built the canal to go.

Every cell owns its own metal. A canal is not a pipe with one shared pool - each block holds what is standing in it, and each tick some of it moves to the next cell along. That is why a long canal takes visible time to deliver, and why a canal left standing full slowly goes solid: metal cools where it sits. A solidified cell is not lost, but you will be chiselling it out.

The pieces:
- Canal Start - sits under a furnace tap and takes the runout
- Canal (straight, bend, T-junction, cross) - the run itself
- Canal Tap - drains the run out; park a barrel under it to fill
- Mold Pedestal - pours into a mold set on it, which is how you cast
- Molten Barrel - a standalone vessel for holding a heat

Building a run. Every canal shape can be cut from cobblestone, from coloured running brick, or from fire brick - hammered and chiselled over fire clay. The rock or brick you use is cosmetic; pick whichever you have. A T-junction forks a heat between two stations, which is how one tap feeds a mold and a barrel at once.

Taps are shut by default. A closed tap severs the run at that point, so metal backs up behind it instead of draining. Open it with rightmouse when you actually want the run to empty.

Casting. Set a mold on a Mold Pedestal and the pedestal pours into it from the canal it is fed by. Cast iron parts, ingots and tool blanks all come out this way. What you can cast depends on what is in the canal - pig from the blast furnace, cast iron from the cupola.

Slope is not modelled. Metal moves along connectors, not downhill, so a canal can run level. What it cannot do is cross a gap: every cell must touch the next.
handbook-designtable-title: Ironworking: Diagrams and the Design Table
handbook-designtable-text:
The Design Table is where plans are drawn. A diagram is a reusable crafting plan: it goes in the grid alongside the raw material, tells the recipe which shape to make, and - because it is a tool, not an ingredient - it is not consumed. Draw a plan once and build from it forever.

Why bother. Without diagrams, every shape of every part needs its own grid pattern, and a pipe network's four shapes across three material tiers is twelve patterns to memorise. With them there is one pattern per part - plan plus material - and the plan picks the shape. The same straight-canal diagram cuts a straight canal out of any rock you feed it.

Blocks required:
- 1 x Design Table

Using a diagram. Put it in the crafting grid with the material the recipe calls for - for a molten canal, cobblestone. The output takes the shape the diagram names and the material you supplied, and the diagram comes back out unharmed.

This is a young system. The molten canal shapes are the first parts to use it, and more will move over. Existing hand-patterned recipes keep working alongside it, so nothing you have already learned stops working.

handbook-steampower-text:
Low Pressure Expanded lets you generate mechanical power from nothing more than boiling water, by laying out pipe networks and bolting together modular steam machinery. It is powerful but demanding: the materials are expensive and a mismanaged boiler can end in a catastrophic explosion, so it is best attempted once you are well established and into the iron age. Everything you build follows one chain - a water supply feeds a boiler, the boiler drives an engine, and the engine turns a single sub-machine - and your goal is to close that chain into a loop that feeds itself while it burns coal. This article explains the pipes that tie it all together; the machines themselves are covered in Steam Power: Boilers, Steam Power: Engines and Steam Power: Fittings.

Any pipes you connect together form a single network that shares one pool. A network carries only one medium at a time - either a gas (air, exhaust or steam) or water, never both at once - and every pipe contributes 30 L of capacity to the shared total. The pressure you see, measured in atmospheres (atm), is simply the stored volume divided by that capacity, and the whole network also settles to a single temperature.

The material a pipe is made of decides how much pressure it can hold: an iron pipe bursts above 5 atm while a stronger steel pipe holds up to 10 atm, and because the weakest pipe sets the limit for the whole run, a single iron section caps an otherwise steel line. An over-pressured run survives for a short while before its pipes begin to fail.

Open ends are the other thing to watch. Any pipe connector left unconnected bleeds the network - roughly 8 L/s of gas or 10 L/s of water - so a leaking run can never build pressure beyond 1 atm, and you should always cap a run against a machine port, a valve or an outlet. Even when sealed, standing water slowly evaporates from pipes and boilers at about 50 L per day.

Laying pipe is mostly automatic: straights, bends and T- and X-junctions snap to face their neighbours as you place them, and if a piece guesses wrong you can spin it with a wrench. To feed a machine, butt a pipe directly against its port face - the boiler outlets, the engine inlets, and the pump and intake flanges.

Two client-side .exmod commands help while you build. .exmod network hi tints every networked block, giving each separate network its own translucent colour so you can see at a glance which pipes share a run and where a connection has broken, and it updates live as you work; .exmod network unhi turns it back off. .exmod measure reports your current display units, and .exmod measure metric or .exmod measure imperial switches between litres, atmospheres and degrees Celsius and gallons, psi and degrees Fahrenheit - a change to the display only, with no effect on the simulation.
handbook-boilers-text:
A boiler burns coal beside a water vessel and forces the resulting steam into a pipe network; every litre of water boils into 16 L of steam at 160-220 °C, which builds up inside the boiler and across the steam network attached to it. To build one, place the boiler block and right-click it (rightmouse) repeatedly with the required materials in your hotbar to raise it through its construction stages. It also needs a masonry firebox around its base; hold ctrl + shift + rightmouse to show the build outline, and the chat will tell you which blocks are still missing.

The Cornish Boiler is the one to start with - a simple single-flue boiler that supplies low-pressure steam, enough to get your first machines turning. Raising it consumes 24 metal plates, 18 nails-and-strips and 8 rods (iron or steel) together with 48 fire bricks, and its firebox is walled from 33 fire-brick blocks fitted with a coke-oven door, two fire-brick pipe passthroughs, a passthrough bend and a pipe outlet (both facing up), leaving one slot open for the coal pile. It pushes up to 32 L/s of steam and chokes at 5 atm; its vessel holds 800 L but needs at least 150 L present before it will boil.

Getting a boiler running is a manual affair at first. You prime it by hand with buckets of water, and once it is making steam that steam can drive the engine behind a fluid pump, which then refills the vessel automatically - the trick is to reach the pressure your engine needs before the hand-poured water runs dry. Once that loop catches, the pumping engine keeps your boilers topped up for as long as the coal burns. In practice you hold rightmouse on the lid to open it, pour in water - from buckets, or piped under pressure into the intake from a fluid pump - and close the lid again; then you lay a coal pile in the firebox slot behind the door and set it alight, and after about three minutes of heating the boiler starts to boil and sends steam out of its top outlet toward your engines. All the while the firebox must breathe: vent its exhaust outlet through a chimney or pipe, because if the back-pressure there climbs above ~0.8 atm the fire goes out.

Boilers are dangerous. One that keeps firing with nowhere to send its steam sits at its choke pressure and can explode. Your emergency release is the lid - opening it vents steam harmlessly at around 100 L/s. An unpiped steam outlet merely leaks, which is not enough to save an over-pressured boiler, and feeding pressurised water into a boiling vessel flashes it to extra steam and spikes the pressure, so always throttle or gate any pumped feedwater. Beware in particular that a Cornish boiler's 5 atm ceiling sits above the Watt engine's 4 atm breaking point: put a pressure valve between them, with an overflow pipe, to keep the engine safe.
handbook-engines-text:
An engine draws steam from a pipe network and uses it to drive a single attached sub-machine. Place the engine first - it rises through right-click construction stages just like a boiler - then set its sub-machine in the cell directly beneath the beam's pumping rod, where it snaps itself into the correct facing.

The Watt Engine runs on large volumes of low-pressure steam. It is cheap enough to be your first steam engine, and a single Cornish boiler can power one safely. It wants 2-4 atm of inlet steam - above 4 atm it wears quickly and can break - and at that pressure it draws 30 L/s of steam and delivers 0.3 units of power (an internal value, enough to run two helve hammers without slowing), while dribbling about 1 L/s of hot condensate from its drain that you can pipe away to reclaim or leave to spill. Building it through its stages takes 4 metal plates, 24 rods and 12 nails-and-strips, all iron or steel, plus 36 fire bricks.

A sub-machine is the block that actually spends the engine's power (one per engine, seated in its drive cell); the engine only provides the power, so what gets done depends on which sub-machine you fit. The Mechanical Power Generator converts that power into turning force for axles, holding a steady speed as long as the load stays within the engine's rated output and overstressing to a halt only if the connected network drags it past roughly double that load. The Fluid Pump moves water from its intake line to its output line at about 5 L/s on a fully-powered engine, pressurising the output to roughly 75% of the engine's inlet steam pressure - enough to lift water into a boiler - and moving twice as much when driven by an overclocked Cornish engine. The Air Blower (from Steelmaking Expanded) instead pressurises air for the blast furnace and Bessemer converter, again up to about 75% of the inlet steam pressure, delivering roughly 16 L/s on a normally-running engine and double that from a pressured-up Cornish.

Pushed beyond its pressure band for too long, an engine breaks: the cylinder bursts and the piston is damaged. Right-click it (rightmouse) with a wrench in hand to see the repair bill, then again with those materials in your hotbar to mend it.
handbook-fittings-text:
This article gathers the smaller blocks that shape and control a pipe network.

A Valve is a hand-operated shut-off in a line. Right-clicking it (rightmouse) toggles it: while open the line flows through, and while closed the network is severed at the valve so the two sides act independently. It sits flush against a machine port.

A Pressure Valve is a one-way overflow. It holds its input side back until the pressure there rises above its gate pressure, then lets the excess spill through to its output side; a wrench flips its direction, and right-clicking it (rightmouse, or ctrl + rightmouse) raises or lowers the gate. With nothing piped to its output it simply vents the excess like a leak. It is the essential regulator between a strong boiler and a weaker engine, and its input side is marked by a copper-textured ring.

A Steam Condenser turns spent steam back into water for reuse. It pulls up to 30 L/s of steam from its steam port and adds the condensed water - one litre for every sixteen litres of steam - to a separate water line that runs through it, letting you reclaim boiler feedwater and relieve steam pressure at the same time.

A Fluid Intake draws fresh water from open water into the network. It must sit directly on a full cube of water at least three blocks deep, and it refuses to work within six blocks of another intake; feed its output into a fluid pump to lift the water onward.

The Manual Fluid Pump is a hand-cranked pump that needs no engine - look for the crank support in its model, as the side it sits on is the input side. Hold rightmouse to crank it, and as long as a working fluid intake feeds its input line it pushes about 2 L/s of water into the output at up to 1 atm. It is the way to prime a boiler's vessel before you have any steam power, and to keep that vessel topped up while pressure builds for the engines.

Finally, passthroughs and outlets are masonry blocks cast around a length of pipe, so the walls of a structure - boiler fireboxes and furnaces - can be built straight across a pipe run. An outlet ends a run at a machine's port face; or, capped with an ordinary chimney stood upright on top of it, it instead vents the network's gas to the sky at about 16 L/s - the standard way to exhaust a firebox.
handbook-steampowerguide-text:
This is a quick walkthrough of the smallest self-sufficient steam line.

Begin with water: place a Fluid Intake on a pond, on a full three-deep block of water beneath it. Next comes the boiler - build a Cornish Boiler with its firebox, fill it with water by bucket or with a Manual Fluid Pump, light a coal pile behind its door, and vent the firebox outlet through a chimney. Then add the engine: raise a Watt Engine nearby and pipe the boiler's steam outlet to its inlet through a Pressure Valve gated at around 2-3 atm, since the Cornish boiler can out-pressure the Watt.

The last piece is the sub-machine in the engine's drive cell. If you drop in a Fluid Pump, pipe the fluid intake into its intake side and run its output up into the boiler, and the water loop closes on itself; if you drop in a Mechanical Power Generator instead, hook its axles up to your helve hammers or other machines. Run the engine's condensate drain back toward the boiler whenever you are short of water, and the result is a steam plant that feeds itself.

From this foundation you can chain on more boilers and engines for greater power, or move up to the high-pressure tier from High Pressure Expanded - a Lancashire Boiler feeding a Cornish Engine. The best use for steam power right now is to drive the machines behind Steelmaking Expanded - the air blowers of the blast furnace and the Bessemer converter - so you can turn out the iron and steel your industrial revolution will demand.
